title: Diverse bacterial pattern recognition receptors sense the core phage proteome.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed 4 spreadsheets. Source Data Fig. 5a (162 KB): 218 phage genes x 21 sensor columns = 4,578 values, 0 missing, full DNA sequence inline for all 218 (327-3,660 bp, all A/C/G/T, 218 unique). Source Data Fig. 2d/ED Fig. 8 (353 KB): 510 constructs x 20 sensors = 10,200 values, 0 missing, DNA inline, sum of the '# Genes' column = exactly 600 across exactly 36 phages. Merged on DNA sequence: 11,858 unique (phage construct, sensor) pairs, 582 unique constructs, 21 sensors; 114 strong hits at q<0.1 (0.96%), 196 at q<0.3. 146 constructs appear in both screens, giving 2,920 repeated pairs: Spearman 0.847, Pearson 0.963, 100% agreement on the binary hit call at q<0.1. Supplementary Tables xlsx (28 MB, 14 sheets): Table S6 has 118 cloned sensors with NCBI accession, full protein sequence (652-2,092 aa) and cloned DNA for every row, and 19 of the 21 screen column names match a row by name. Table S2 lists 359,879 STAND representatives, Table S5 178,641 proteins with structure cluster and AlphaFold DB columns. Also read Methods: q = (mNeonGreen-normalised barcode count with the sensor) / (same count in the empty-vector control).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That EcAvs8 and EcDsr1 (the 2 of 21 sensor columns I could not match by name in Table S6) are previously published systems whose sequences are recoverable from NCBI. That some library genes were dropped for basal toxicity in E. coli. The existence and contents of the independent Nature Microbiology 2026 trigger screen proposed for external validation — I did not open its files (the publisher page redirected to a login).

a1_downloadable.note: All four spreadsheets downloaded anonymously from Springer static content in one pass; no login, no application. Checked in the files.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: The label is literally a cell: each sensor is a column, each phage gene a row, and the cell holds the measured toxicity ratio q. Nothing to construct.

a3_inputs_present.note: Full DNA sequence inline for all 582 phage constructs; full protein sequence inline for 118 cloned sensors in Table S6. Only 2 of 21 sensors need an NCBI accession lookup.

a4_units_stated.note: Methods define q = normalised barcode count with sensor / count in empty-vector control; dimensionless, 1 = no effect, 0 = full depletion. An 'Empty' control column sits in both files (median 0.999).

a5_enough_rows.note: 11,858 unique sensor x phage-protein pairs counted in the merged files. Caveat: only 114 are strong hits (0.96%), so the usable positive set is small.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~30 MB of spreadsheets; ~600 protein sequences to embed
a6_fits_laptop.note: Entire usable dataset is under 30 MB and parsed in seconds on this laptop. No GPU needed for a frozen-embedding baseline.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Paper says 600 genes/36 phages: the file sums to exactly 600 across exactly 36 phages. Paper says 4,360 pairs from 218 targets x 18 Avs: 218 x 20 Avs columns (excluding the non-Avs EcDsr1) = 4,360 exactly.

a8_label_provenance.note: Label is a physical measurement: colony survival after co-expression, read out by Illumina barcode counting. Not a model output and not computable from the sequence features.

B1.why: Three files join cleanly: two screen matrices on exact DNA sequence (146 exact matches), sensor sequences from Table S6 by name.

B2.why: All four xlsx files parsed with pandas on the first try, zero missing cells in both screen matrices.

B3.why: One assay, one lab, one normalisation (mNeonGreen plus empty-vector control); authors already produced the ratio q.

B4.why: No missing values, but q=0 is a floor (full depletion) and some genes were dropped for basal toxicity.

B5.why: 146 constructs measured in both screens; dedupe is an exact string match on DNA sequence, and they agree (Spearman 0.847).

B6.why: Column headers are bare sensor names; the definition of q lives only in Methods, not in the file.

C1.why: Asking how far recognition extends across homologues of one fold is informative whether the model works or not.

C2.why: Searched: no model predicts which phage protein triggers which defence sensor; DefensePredictor solves a different task.

C3.why: Novel plus unique-application: these 11,858 measured pairs have never been modelled; nobody has an ML trigger predictor.

C4.why: Each pair costs cloning, barcoding, transformation, plating and deep sequencing; this screen took a whole Nature paper.

C5.why: Obvious dummies I computed from the files: 0.96% prevalence, and a cognate-family lookup at 31% precision / 93% recall.

D1.why: ESM-2, an open-weight protein language model, matches both sides of the pair; all sequences are amino-acid strings.

D2.why: ~603 sequences to embed once on CPU, then a small head; no fine-tuning needed.

D3.why: ESM-2 weights are MIT licensed; the Nature article is open access with source data provided.

E1.why: Can cluster the 582 phage proteins at 40% identity and hold out clusters; also hold out whole phages and whole Avs families.

E2.why: Seen in the files: 47 phages, 23 target protein families, 23 sensor group names in Table S6.

E3.why: Always-negative dummy gives 0.96% precision; the cognate-family lookup rule gives 106/337 precision, both computed from the files.

E4.why: 2,920 pairs measured twice across the two screens: Spearman 0.847, 100% binary agreement at q<0.1.

E5.why: Must recover the published Avs3/Avs2 to large terminase and Avs7/Avs8/Avs10 to major capsid protein pairings.

E6.why: Label shuffling within each sensor column and sensor-only / target-only feature ablations are both trivially runnable.

E7.why: An independent 2026 Nature Microbiology trigger screen (>400 phage genes x 39 E. coli strains) exists; I did not open its files.

E8.why: No published predictive-performance number for this task; the paper reports AlphaFold3 ipTM only for confirmed hits, never on negatives.

G1.why: NCBI protein accessions (WP_...) for all sensors, GenBank accessions for new phages, AlphaFold DB column in Table S5.

G2.why: AlphaFold DB and UniProt on sensor accession; the INPHARED phage genome collection on phage protein family.

G3.why: Sensor accession to AlphaFold structure is one-to-one; phage protein to phage genome is a clean one-to-many.

G4.why: Which of the 359,879 catalogued STAND sensors senses which phage protein family — neither table answers that alone.

H1.why: 11,744 explicit measured non-hits alongside 114 hits, plus empty-vector controls; negatives are the bulk of the file.

H2.why: 36-47 phages and sensors from 11 bacterial genera, but every assay ran in one E. coli host, one lab, one plate format.

H3.why: Honest claim writes out in one sentence (see honest_claim_h3); the restriction to E. coli-expressible genes is explicit.

H4.why: Paper states the gaps: genes dropped for basal toxicity, and Avs22-24 for which no activator was found.

I1.why: The Gao lab (Stanford), Sorek lab (Weizmann), Laub lab (MIT) and Kranzusch lab all run trigger screens like this one.

I2.why: A ranked trigger list tells a lab which handful of phage genes to clone first instead of screening hundreds.

I3.why: Precision among the top 10 ranked candidates is exactly the decision: which genes go into the next cloning round.

I4.why: A cognate-family lookup already recovers 106 of 114 hits; ML only earns its place on within-family discrimination.

J1.why: Grouped splits, frozen protein language model embeddings, severe class imbalance, calibration — all real modelling work.

J2.why: All ground-truth pairings are named in the paper, and the authors are at the same institution as the user.

J3.why: The cleaned 11,858-pair table is the first ML-ready benchmark for defence-sensor trigger prediction, useful even if the model is mediocre.

J4.why: Three weeks: one to build the table and embeddings, one to model, one to write up.

J5.why: Kill condition drafted here (within-family AUPRC below 0.35 after two weeks) but not yet written into NOTES.md.

existing_models.name: DefensePredictor (DeWeirdt et al., Science 2026; bioRxiv 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Classifies a bacterial protein as anti-phage defensive or not, from ESM-2 (a protein language model) embeddings plus gradient boosting. Reported: applied to 69 E. coli strains, 42 predictions experimentally validated, ~45% of tested predictions conferred protection. No split reported for trigger prediction, because it does not do trigger prediction.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Which phage molecule activates each newly discovered system remains unknown; they discover systems but not what the systems sense.

existing_models.name: AlphaFold-Multimer / AlphaFold3 co-folding with interface predicted template modelling (ipTM) score
existing_models.score_and_split: Used inside this very paper: confident ipTM 0.71-0.91 for 11 of 13 sensor-target complexes. A separate Molecular Cell 2025 study screened ~2 million phage genomes this way against defence proteins and reported roughly a 50% hit rate on follow-up. Neither reports a score on a defined negative set, so there is no published precision-recall number for this task.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Distinguishing true sensor-target pairs from decoys at scale; ipTM has never been calibrated against measured non-binders.

existing_models.name: Strain-level phage-host interaction predictors (Nature Microbiology 2026; Scientific Reports 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: AUROC 0.67-0.94 across six datasets (115,037 interactions, 949 bacterial strains, 518 phages) for predicting whether a phage infects a bacterial strain from genomes. Different task — whole-organism infection, not which protein activates which sensor.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Mechanistic basis of the predictions; they predict infection outcome without identifying the molecular recognition events.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (esm2_t33_650M_UR50D), a protein language model from Meta
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU; ~603 sequences embedded once (582 phage proteins plus 21 sensors), cached to disk, then a logistic-regression or gradient-boosting head.
backbone.licence: MIT (permissive). The paper's source data is open access with the Nature article.

integration.partner_dataset: AlphaFold DB (predicted structures, joinable on the NCBI/UniProt accessions in Supplementary Tables S5 and S6) and the INPHARED phage genome collection (phage structural protein families); Supplementary Table S2's own 359,879 catalogued STAND sensors are the application target.
integration.join_key: NCBI protein accession (WP_... / HBS... / SDE...) for sensors; phage protein sequence or phage GenBank accession (PX985120-PX985132) for targets.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Which phage protein family does each of the 359,879 catalogued but uncharacterised prokaryotic STAND sensors recognise, and which circulating phages carry a variant of that protein that escapes detection?

controls.positive_control: The model must rediscover the already-published pairings in the data: Avs2 and Avs3 triggered by the large terminase (11/18 and 12/18 terminase homologues, counted in the file), and Avs7, Avs8 and Avs10 triggered by the major capsid protein. Plus a plumbing control: predict protein length from the embedding, which must be near-perfect.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the q values within each sensor column and confirm precision-recall area under the curve collapses to the 0.96% prevalence; ablate to sensor-only features (should be useless for ranking targets) and target-only features; replace embeddings with random vectors of the same shape.
controls.external_validation: The independent trigger screen in Nature Microbiology 2026 (>400 phage genes across 39 E. coli strains carrying different defence systems, >100 trigger-system pairs reported, including lambda gpE major capsid protein activating Avs8). Also in-house: the 27 extra genes in Supplementary Table S13 and the plaque assays against 12 coliphages. I did not open the Nature Microbiology files.

honest_claim_h3: Among phage protein-coding genes that can be expressed in E. coli without killing it on their own, and for the 21 sensor constructs assayed in this one lab's plate-based co-expression screen, the model ranks which homologues of a sensor's cognate target fold actually trigger cell death.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the sequences of a bacterial immune sensor and a phage protein to predict whether the sensor detects that protein and kills the cell.
plain_idea.train_on: Pairs of (bacterial sensor protein sequence, phage protein sequence). I counted 11,858 unique pairs in the files: 582 distinct phage gene constructs from 36-47 phages, each tested against 21 sensor constructs representing about 15 sensor families.
plain_idea.predict: A number called q, which is how much a phage gene's barcode is depleted from surviving colonies when co-expressed with the sensor, relative to an empty-vector control. q near 1 means nothing happened; q near 0 means the sensor fired and the cell died. Measured by Illumina barcode counting.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Labs that discover new bacterial immune systems currently have to clone and screen hundreds of phage genes to find out what each system senses; a ranked shortlist would cut that to a handful. Even a failed model would show that recognition depends on structural detail sequence embeddings cannot see, which supports the paper's own shape-complementarity conclusion.

more_or_better_data.why: 11,858 directly measured sensor-by-phage-protein pairs with 11,744 explicit negatives. DefensePredictor was trained on a different label entirely (is a protein defensive), and AlphaFold co-folding uses no task-specific training data at all. No comparable labelled table of measured non-recognition exists.

confidence_score.why: 2,920 pairs were measured twice across the two screens (Spearman 0.847, 100% binary agreement), and 73 constructs carry 2-3 barcodes, so measurement noise is estimable and AlphaFold ipTM offers nothing comparable. But with only 21 sensors there is too little data to calibrate confidence per sensor family.

models_beatable.why: DefensePredictor is not a competitor — different task. AlphaFold3 co-folding is genuinely strong (ipTM 0.71-0.91 on the 11 confirmed complexes in this paper) but was never scored against negatives and costs GPU-hours per pair; a CPU model that matches its ranking at a thousandth the cost is a real win.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition: no existing model can be run as our baseline on the same split in an afternoon. AlphaFold3 weights are access-restricted and GPU-bound, so the comparison would be against published ipTM values for hits only, not a matched evaluation.

label_elsewhere.sources: Searched and found: the Nature Microbiology 2026 phage protein screen (>400 phage genes x 39 E. coli strains, >100 trigger-system pairs); Gao et al., Science 2022 (triggers for Avs1-4); Molecular Cell 2025 proteome-wide AlphaFold2 anti-defence screen. DefenseFinder and PADLOC catalogue defence systems but not their triggers. No single large resource collects measured sensor-trigger pairs.
label_elsewhere.join_key: Protein amino-acid sequence, or NCBI protein accession for the sensor side.
label_elsewhere.why: Several independent screens have measured the same kind of label, so a model trained here can be tested on data from a different lab, but they are scattered across supplementary tables rather than pooled in one database.

risks: Near-duplicate phage proteins: the 22 major capsid proteins include homologues from nine closely related Drexlerviridae phages, so a random split would put almost identical sequences in both train and test.
The same construct was measured in both screens (146 constructs, 2,920 repeated pairs); naively stacking the two tables puts an identical row on both sides of the split.
Only 21 distinct sensors exist, so a model given sensor embeddings can effectively memorise sensor identity and recover its hit rows rather than learn recognition.
The functional annotation column ('MCP', 'portal', ...) is a near-perfect shortcut to the answer; using it as a feature would hide whether the model learned anything from sequence.
54 of 510 rows in the first screen are multi-gene constructs (2-6 genes), so which gene caused the depletion is ambiguous and the label is partly mis-assigned.
leakage_plan.split: Three nested grouped splits, all built from columns I saw in the files: (1) cluster the 582 phage protein sequences with MMseqs2 at 40% identity and hold out whole clusters; (2) hold out whole phages using the 'Phage' column (47 values in the Fig. 5a file, 36 in the Fig. 2d file); (3) hold out whole sensor families using the 'Group Name' column of Supplementary Table S6 (23 groups), which prevents SeAvs7/Se2Avs7 and KpAvs20/Kp2Avs20 from splitting across folds.
checks: Shuffle q within each sensor column and confirm precision-recall area under the curve collapses to the 0.96% prevalence baseline.
Report, for every test-set hit, the maximum sequence identity to any training-set hit for the same sensor; if it is routinely above 70%, the model is doing nearest-neighbour lookup.
Train on the sensor embedding alone and on the annotation column alone; both must fail at ranking targets within a sensor.
Deduplicate on exact DNA sequence before any split, and confirm the 146 shared constructs land in one fold.
leakage_plan.verdict: Manageable — every grouping column I need is already in the files — but the 21-sensor ceiling makes sensor-side memorisation the serious risk, so the honest evaluation has to be leave-one-sensor-family-out with only about 15 folds.

success_criteria.metric: Two numbers. Primary: precision among the top 10 phage proteins ranked for each held-out sensor, because the decision a lab makes is 'which ten genes do I clone next'. Secondary: precision-recall area under the curve on the 337-pair within-cognate-family task (does this particular homologue of the right fold actually trigger?), because that is where a lookup rule gives no answer.
success_criteria.baselines: Computed by me from the files: always-negative dummy = 0.96% prevalence on the full 11,858-pair matrix; cognate-family lookup rule = 106 hits out of 337 cognate-family pairs, i.e. 31% precision at 93% recall (106 of 114 hits). No published model number exists for this task.
success_criteria.success: Within-cognate-family precision-recall area under the curve of at least 0.55 under 40%-identity clustered splits, against the 0.31 prevalence baseline, AND top-10 precision of at least 0.5 per sensor when whole phages are held out.
success_criteria.noise_ceiling: Binary label is essentially noise-free: the 2,920 pairs measured in both screens agree 100% on the hit call at q<0.1. For regression on q, the ceiling is Spearman ~0.85 (the cross-screen replicate correlation I measured).
success_criteria.kill: If within-cognate-family precision-recall area under the curve stays below 0.35 (no better than prevalence) under clustered splits after two weeks, stop and publish the benchmark table plus the negative result.

ambitious.why: Publishes biology-first machine learning with experimental consequence; would need the model to nominate the trigger of a sensor family it never saw and have that call confirmed against the independent Nature Microbiology screen.

realistic.why: Publishes new benchmarks with honest baselines; the likely outcome — a curated 11,858-pair trigger-prediction benchmark plus an ESM-2 baseline that beats the family-lookup rule on within-family discrimination but not dramatically — is exactly its scope.

fallback.why: Takes resource-and-negative-result papers; even if the model fails, the cleaned sensor-trigger table with grouped splits and the finding that sequence embeddings cannot separate triggering from non-triggering homologues is a publishable contribution.

pitch.headline: 11,858 measured pairs of bacterial immune sensor against phage protein, with 11,744 explicit non-hits — the first labelled table of what bacterial immunity does not sense.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Negatives dominate: 114 hits among 11,858 pairs, all from one assay and one normalisation, with zero missing cells. 146 constructs were measured twice and agree 100% on the hit call. Every sequence is inline, no accession lookups.
pitch.the_win: Beat the cognate-family lookup rule's 31% precision (106 of 337, computed from the files) on deciding which homologues of the right fold actually trigger, under 40%-identity clustered splits.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: A clean negative: that sequence alone cannot say which homologue of a conserved fold triggers a sensor, which supports the paper's own claim that recognition is shape complementarity, and tells the field to spend compute on structure instead.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Gao lab at Stanford, the Sorek lab at Weizmann and the Laub lab at MIT, all of whom run these screens by hand; it would change which phage genes they clone first for a newly found defence system.

ml_idea: Freeze ESM-2 (a protein language model), embed the 582 phage protein sequences and the 21 sensor sequences once on CPU, and train a small head on the concatenated pair embedding to predict the measured toxicity ratio q, as both a binary hit call and a regression. Evaluate under three grouped splits built from columns in the files: 40%-identity sequence clusters of the phage proteins, whole held-out phages, and whole held-out sensor families. Report two tasks separately: the easy all-pairs ranking (where a family-annotation lookup is already strong) and the hard within-cognate-family discrimination of 337 pairs with 106 hits, where no lookup helps. Then apply the trained model to Supplementary Table S2's 359,879 catalogued STAND sensors to nominate triggers for uncharacterised families.

effort.compute_note: Spreadsheet parsing and the merge were timed here: seconds. Embedding time is an estimate — 603 sequences averaging roughly 500 residues through ESM-2 650M on CPU at a few seconds each, with the longest sensor (2,092 residues) needing windowing, which sets the 4 GB peak. Cross-validation time is estimated for a gradient-boosting head on 11,858 rows across about 20 grouped folds.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Cluster the 582 phage protein sequences at 40% identity and count, for each sensor, how many distinct clusters contain a hit. If most sensors have hits in fewer than 3 clusters, the within-family task is just recognising near-duplicates and the interesting half of the project is dead — one MMseqs2 run, under 30 minutes.

verdict_reason: Every Part A killer verified directly in the files, not from the paper: the label is a cell in a matrix (measured colony depletion, not a model output), both sequences are inline, units are defined precisely in Methods, counts match the paper exactly (600 genes / 36 phages / 4,360 pairs), and the whole usable dataset is 30 MB. The field is genuinely empty — three searches found no model that predicts which phage protein triggers which bacterial sensor, only DefensePredictor (a different task) and AlphaFold co-folding (GPU-bound, never scored on negatives). Negatives are the bulk of the data, which is rare and valuable; a cross-screen replicate set of 2,920 pairs gives a real noise floor; and an independent trigger screen exists for external validation. The honest weakness is that only 114 of 11,858 pairs are hits and a simple family-annotation lookup recovers 106 of them, so the project's value rests on the harder within-family question (337 pairs, 106 hits) and on only about 15 held-out sensor families. Run the 30-minute clustering check first.
